svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. The hundred point scorecard, reweighted by evidential value
svg.desc: A comparison of two scoring schemes for evaluating a VPN provider. The usual scheme awards ten points for jurisdiction, of which three are for not belonging to an intelligence alliance, twenty for technical features that every serious provider now has, and only three for evidence from an actual legal test. The reweighted scheme awards twenty five points for evidence from real testing, twenty for audit quality including type recency and frequency, twenty for architecture that limits what can exist to be handed over, fifteen for traceable ownership, ten for the technical baseline treated as a floor rather than a differentiator, five for jurisdiction measured by current retention law, and five for honest marketing. A band below explains the three changes and why each was made.
svg.text: Figure 3: The Scorecard, Reweighted by What Each Signal Proves
A hundred point rubric looks rigorous. What makes it rigorous or not is whether the weights match how much each item actually tells you.

g.text: Technical features
Modern protocols, leak protection, kill switch
Verification
Of which evidence from a real legal test: 3
Privacy policy wording
Read and scored as text
Jurisdiction
Of which "not in an intelligence alliance": 3
Ownership
Business model
Track record
Marketing honesty
Twenty points for features every serious provider
already has, and three for the only real evidence.
Evidence from real testing
Seizures, warrants, court records. Never tested scores zero, not full marks.
Audit quality
Type, date, scope published, how many, and whether unannounced.
Architecture that limits what exists
Anonymous payment, no identity required to hold an account.
Traceable ownership
Who ultimately owns it, and whether that changed recently.
Technical baseline
A floor to clear, not a differentiator. Everybody has this now.
Jurisdiction
Current retention law only. Alliance membership scores nothing.
Marketing honesty
A cheap signal, and a surprisingly reliable one.
Same hundred points. Different question being answered.

svg.text: Three changes, and the reasoning for each

g.text: Evidence went from 3 to 25. A documented demand that produced nothing is the only signal that settles anything, and it scored below the kill switch.
Technical features went from 20 to 10. In 2015 they separated providers. Today every serious provider has them, so the row no longer discriminates.
Jurisdiction went from 10 to 5, alliance membership to zero. What matters is current retention law, and Lesson 6.1 has one changing right now.
And "never tested" now scores zero rather than being silently ignored, because an untested claim is an absence of information rather than a clean record.

svg.text: Use whichever weighting you like. The point is that a rubric encodes a set of beliefs about what evidence is worth, and most published ones never state theirs.
If you publish a scorecard, publish the reasoning for the weights. That is the part a reader cannot reconstruct and the part that makes it useful.
